title: Continuity and types of discontinuity
section: Continuous Functions ▷ Definition and closure properties
terms: continuity at a point; continuous function; one-sided endpoint continuity; removable discontinuity; jump discontinuity; infinite discontinuity; continuity of a composition.

exposition.text:
A function is continuous at a domain point a when lim f(x) = f(a), with the limit inter-
x→a
preted relative to its domain. On [a, b], endpoint continuity is one-sided. A removable discon-
tinuity has a finite limiting value that can be restored by redefining one value; a jump has un-
equal finite one-sided limits; an infinite discontinuity involves unbounded one-sided behavior.
Sums, products, and compositions preserve continuity where the relevant functions are continu-
ous; quotients do so where the denominator is nonzero. Polynomials are continuous everywhere,
and rational, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions are continuous on their domains. To
join piecewise formulas, match the actual limiting values, not merely the displayed expressions.
Continuity on an open interval alone supplies no boundedness or endpoint attainment.

question.text:

For x ̸= 1, set f (x) = (x − 3x + 2)/(x − 1) . Which value of f(1) makes f continuous?
(A) 0 (B) 1 (C) 2 (D) 3 (E) No such value exists.

solution.text:
3 2
x − 3x + 2 = (x − 1) (x + 2), so the punctured formula is x + 2. Its limit at 1 is 3, uniquely
determining the extension.

question.text:
Let f(x) = sin x for x < 0, f (0) = c, and f (x) = log(1 + ax) for x > 0, on a sufficiently small
neighborhood of zero. For which pairs (a, c) is f continuous at zero?
(A) Only (1, 0) (B) Only (0, 0)
(C) All real a with c = 0 (D) All real c with a = 1
(E) All real (a, c)

solution.text:
Both one-sided limits equal zero for every fixed real a; the logarithm is defined near zero
because 1+ax > 0 there. Continuity therefore requires and is guaranteed by c = 0. Matching
slopes would be an additional differentiability condition.

question.text:
For x ∈/ {0, 1, 2}, let f(x) = |x|/x + 1/(x − 1). Which describes the exceptional points 0, 1, 2,
respectively?
(A) Removable hole, infinite behavior, jump
(B) Jump, infinite behavior, removable hole
(C) Jump, removable hole, infinite behavior
(D) Infinite behavior, jump, removable hole
(E) Three removable holes

solution.text:
At zero the left and right limits are −2 and 0, so no assigned value can remove the jump.
At 1, the reciprocal term has infinite one-sided limits. At 2, both limits equal 2, so defining
f(2) = 2 fills the hole. These are classifications of the excluded locations, not failures of
continuity relative to the existing domain.

question.text:
2 2
At how many real points is f(x) = (x − 1)/(x − x), on its natural domain, discontinuous relative
to that domain?
(A) 1 (B) Infinitely many (C) 2 (D) 0 (E) 3

solution.text:
A rational function is continuous at every point of its domain. The excluded points 0, 1 are
not domain points, so relative-domain continuity fails nowhere.

question.text:
Define f(0) = 0 and f (x) = x sin(1/x) otherwise. Which is true at zero?
(A) Unbounded near zero
(B) Continuous but not differentiable
(C) Differentiable with derivative 1
(D) Differentiable with derivative 0
(E) A jump discontinuity occurs

solution.text:
The bound |f(x)| ≤ |x| proves continuity. But f(x)/x = sin(1/x) has no limit, so the
derivative does not exist.

question.text:

Define f : [0, 1] → R by f(0) = a, f(1) = b, and f (x) = x/(1 + x) for 0 < x < 1. Which (a, b)
makes f continuous on its entire domain?
(A) (0, 0)
(B) (0, 1/2)
(C) (1, 1/2)
(D) (0, 1)
(E) No pair, because two-sided limits at the endpoints are unavailable.

solution.text:
Continuity is relative to [0, 1]. The right-hand limit at 0 is zero and the left-hand limit at
1 is 1/2. Assigning these endpoint values gives continuity everywhere; values outside the
domain are irrelevant.
